alignment.note: Greek ἀνέπεσαν ('they reclined') is a finite aorist; the Peshitta ܘܐܣܬܡܟܘ (Ethpaal of s-m-k, 'they were made to recline') carries the conjunction within the verb itself, so the same single token serves both the 'and' and the verb. Latin discubuerunt matches the Greek deponent sense closely.

Greek doubles the noun πρασιαὶ πρασιαὶ ('garden-plot by garden-plot'), a Semitic distributive reduplication that the Peshitta faithfully reproduces with ܣܡܟܝܢ ܣܡܟܝܢ ('groups, groups'). The Vulgate flattens this distributive idiom to a single noun in partes, losing the reduplicative force.

Greek uses the distributive preposition κατά repeated before each numeral; Latin distributes this sense across in and per rather than a single recurring preposition, while the Peshitta expresses distribution through reduplication of the numerals rather than any preposition.

The Peshitta renders 'hundred' with a reduplicated pair ܕܡܐܐ ܡܐܐ ('by hundreds, hundreds'), continuing the Semitic distributive pattern, whereas Greek ἑκατόν and Latin centenos use a single distributive numeral form.

The second distributive κατά before 'fifty' has no separate counterpart: Latin uses no repeated preposition (et quinquagenos) and the Peshitta again signals distribution by numeral reduplication rather than a preposition.
As with 'hundred', the Peshitta reduplicates ܘܕܚܡܫܝܢ ܚܡܫܝܢ ('and by fifties, fifties') to convey the distributive sense, while Greek πεντήκοντα and Latin quinquagenos employ a single numeral form.
